scenes.heading: Algorithms and flowcharts
scenes.sub: Clear steps, in order, every time
scenes.say: A recipe, the steps to set up a phone, the way you add big numbers in columns. They are all algorithms. Let's learn how to follow them and draw them.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A pancake recipe: ingredients in, steps, pancakes out
scenes.science: An algorithm: input in, process steps, output out
scenes.breaks: a recipe can say 'cook until golden', which people read differently. A maths algorithm must be exact.
scenes.say: Think of a recipe for pancakes. Ingredients go in, you follow the steps in order, and pancakes come out. An algorithm is the same: an input goes in, you do the process, and an output comes out. But unlike a recipe, every step must be exact, so everyone gets the same answer.

scenes.heading: A good algorithm
points: Every step has only one meaning
Steps are done in a set order
Same input gives the same output
scenes.say: A good algorithm has steps with only one meaning. The steps are done in a set order. It always finishes. And the same input always gives the same output.

scenes.heading: Flowchart shapes
scenes.say: A flowchart draws an algorithm with shapes and arrows. Ovals start and end it. Slanted boxes, called parallelograms, bring numbers in and out. Rectangles are actions, like add seven. Diamonds ask a yes or no question, and you follow only one arrow out.

scenes.heading: Run it forwards
scenes.question: Start → Input x → Add 7 → Multiply by 2 → Output. Find the output when x = 12.
scenes.say: Input twelve. Follow the arrows. Add seven to get nineteen. Multiply by two to get thirty-eight. The output is thirty-eight. Notice you add first, because the arrows say so.
scenes.caption: Input 12. Follow the arrows. 12 + 7 = 19. 19 × 2 = 38. The output is 38. Notice you add first, because the arrows say so.

scenes.heading: Run it backwards
scenes.question: Multiply by 4, then subtract 6. The output is 30. What was the input?
scenes.say: Now backwards. An algorithm multiplies by four, then subtracts six, and the output is thirty. Undo the last step first: thirty plus six is thirty-six. Then undo the first step: thirty-six divided by four is nine. Check: nine times four, take six, is thirty. The input was nine.
scenes.caption: An algorithm does × 4, then − 6, and the output is 30. Undo the last step first: 30 + 6 = 36. Then 36 ÷ 4 = 9. Check: 9 × 4 − 6 = 30. The input was 9.

scenes.heading: Reverse an algorithm
steps: Work back to the first step
scenes.say: To reverse any algorithm, list the steps, start from the last one, and do the opposite operation each time. It's like shoes and socks: you take your shoes off before your socks. Then check by running your answer forwards.

points: Algorithm: clear steps, in order, that finish
Diamonds decide; ovals open and close
Reverse: undo the last step first
scenes.say: Quick recap. An algorithm is a set of clear steps, in order, that always finishes. Input, process, output. Diamonds decide, ovals open and close. To reverse, undo the last step first. Now try the practice questions!
